source.version_note: Supplied CHI 2022 publisher-style proceedings article, 17 pages, DOI 10.1145/3491102.3517732. Crossref records publication on 27 April 2022 and online publication on 28 April 2022; both support citation year 2022. The PDF creation date is not substituted for publication.
source.verification_method: All 17 text pages read, including the full 146-reference bibliography. Figures 1–3 and their UI/flow/boxplot details visually inspected on pages 9–11; both tables read. Crossref verifies main identity and the cited priority-heuristic and betrayal-aversion records. The European Commission’s public guideline record verifies one institutional/year correction. OSF data, dialog, pretests, analysis code and scale source were not independently read or run.

citation.title: Capable but Amoral? Comparing AI and Human Expert Collaboration in Ethical Decision Making
citation.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, 1–17

reading.source_scope_note: Online Unity simulation with 428 retained nonexpert participants, randomized rescue/defense and advisor/decider framing, and within-person human/AI source blocks. Participants make timed simulated choices and rate trust/responsibility. Advice is scripted and deliberately avoids clear errors; no live AI, actual casualty, objective moral benchmark or real deployment is evaluated.
access_limits: OSF data, full dialog, individual outcomes, MDMT items, pretests, uncertainty calculations and fitted models were not independently read or reproduced. View-only tokens from the supplied paper are not copied into public review records.

The article reports several incompatible degrees of freedom, model descriptions and result statements. Exact sample-specific denominators and paired covariances are not available in the supplied main text.
Cited philosophical books, the MDMT source chapter, betrayal experiments and primary normative-control documents were not fully read. Metadata/header checks do not count as separate reviewed papers.

study.design: Four between-person cells: maximize lives saved versus minimize lives lost, crossed with human-in-the-loop versus human-on-the-loop expert framing. Human versus AI expert is within-person in randomized block order. Each of two source missions contains four decisions; the results sometimes call the four decision positions missions.
study.flow: 850 considered participation; 197 returned, 25 failed initial attention, 141 failed training comprehension, 12 timed out; 475 remained. Forty-seven more lacked timely decision data, yielding 428. The four final cells are 97/103 rescue HITL/HOTL and 101/127 defense HITL/HOTL. Uneven exclusions after assignment affect the analyzed sample.
study.sample: 428 Prolific nonexperts, mean age 26, SD 7.8; 253 women, reported 59%; payment GBP 3.75, mean 31 minutes. Thirty-nine percent report university-level mathematics/probability/physics. Pretest participant counts and raw validation detail are external.
study.task: A rescue drone delivers gas masks or a defense drone intercepts a threatened attack with possible collateral deaths. Three options vary number affected and probability. Time limit 30 seconds. Advisors alternately favor probability/risk or expected-value criteria; advice type is randomized and held comparable across expert labels, with no clearly bad recommendation.
study.control_manipulation: Despite advisor versus decider wording, both configurations use a preselected option and require active change if the participant disagrees. All participants are reminded they ultimately remain responsible. Figure 1 shows a selected target and Veto/Confirm buttons. This is a subtle framing/control package, not a full contrast between active authorization and autonomous action without a human.
study.measures: MDMT overall, capacity and moral trust, with Does Not Fit allowed and remaining applicable items averaged. Trust ratings for human and AI appear together after both blocks. Separate 7-point responsibility ratings for self/human expert versus self/AI/programmer/seller; these are not a fixed-total allocation. Reliance is a binary simulated choice matching the offered option. Several traits are measured after the task.
study.trust_descriptives: AI versus human overall trust 5.36 (SD 1.1) versus 5.11 (.8), capacity 5.66 (1.0) versus 5.15 (.9); moral trust human 5.00 (1.17) versus AI 4.46 (2.2). Printed t tests all use df 854 despite within-person source exposure. These are source-reported directions, not independently validated paired inferences.
study.responsibility_descriptives: Human expert 4.39 (SD 1.8), AI 2.64 (1.8), programmer 3.69 (1.9), seller 3.81 (1.9). Participants remain highly self-responsible in Figure 3. Several paired-test descriptions, dfs, near-equal programmer means and order-effect directions require clarification.
study.reliance: For decision positions 1/2, switches away from human advice are 50%/49% versus AI 52%/55%, with reported paired tests p = .558/.454. Positions 3/4: human 46%/43% versus AI 39%/38%, reported p = .002/<.001. Authors report increased reliance late in both blocks; exact joint counts, repeated-measure models and multiplicity controls are not reproduced. Both source blocks contain only four decisions, not a longitudinal field deployment.
study.autonomy: Reported logistic autonomy coefficient .3693, SE .202, p = .068, CI [−.027,.766]; framing p = .095, order p = .513. Nonsignificance is not equivalence. Responsibility effects largely null except small programmer effects/interactions; discussion reverses one interaction direction.
study.interpretation: The source distinguishes perceptions from real capabilities and admits no moral ground truth. Capability trust and overall trust align with later reliance, so lower moral-facet trust is not a paradox proving reliance contradicts every type of trust. Machine heuristic, performance-driven trust growth and scapegoating are possible explanations/risks, not identified mediators or observed harms.

summary: No new entry. Enrich performance trust, algorithm appreciation/aversion and responsibility attribution with qualified simulation evidence. Keep philosophical moral trust distinct from MDMT integrity/sincerity ratings, and avoid converting distributed ratings into diffusion or actual scapegoating. Correct two bibliography records and document paired-data, sample-df, p-value and interaction-description conflicts without guessing raw corrections.

findings.definition: Expecting an agent or system to perform competently and reliably in a relevant task.
findings.novelty_rationale: An existing concept covers this meaning or its boundary. Keep the stable entry and distinguish the present operationalization rather than create another trust, reliance or responsibility synonym.

evidence.quote: was higher than capacity trust in humans

findings.evidence_scope: Direct MDMT capacity-trust ratings favor the AI label in this controlled simulation despite equal scripted advice quality. The paired-design/df issue limits exact inferential confidence. This is perceived capability, not demonstrated superior AI competence or a causal mediator of later reliance.
findings.boundary: Competence, reliability, moral integrity and actual reliance differ. Higher confidence can be justified or mistaken. A plausible error-free advice sequence does not establish performance under real failure or calibrated trust.

findings.definition: Preferring or weighting algorithmic judgment more than comparable human judgment.
findings.novelty_rationale: An existing concept covers this meaning or its boundary. Keep the stable entry and distinguish the present operationalization rather than create another trust, reliance or responsibility synonym.

evidence.quote: reliance was slightly higher for AI

findings.evidence_scope: Observed simulated choices favor the AI source modestly at later decision positions, with earlier contrasts nonsignificant. Advice quality is held comparable and clear errors are absent. This is a specific source/task pattern, not universal appreciation, verified ethical accuracy or long-term adoption.
findings.boundary: A source preference is not automatically overreliance or fair evidence of better performance. Separate short simulated choices, post-task ratings, source effects and actual capability.

findings.definition: Reluctance to use or accept algorithmic judgments relative to human judgment in a comparable task.
findings.novelty_rationale: An existing concept covers this meaning or its boundary. Keep the stable entry and distinguish the present operationalization rather than create another trust, reliance or responsibility synonym.

evidence.quote: higher moral trust for the human expert

findings.evidence_scope: The predicted lower AI reliance is not supported: choices are similar early and favor AI later. Moral-facet trust favors humans while capacity/overall trust favors AI. Thus one lower subscale is not a general use-avoidance result; statistical and design limits remain.
findings.boundary: Trust dimensions, reliance choices and willingness to give a machine resources differ. Do not infer general aversion from a single moral-integrity rating or infer its universal absence from this simulation.

findings.definition: Assigning fault or responsibility to an agent for a negative event or outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: An existing concept covers this meaning or its boundary. Keep the stable entry and distinguish the present operationalization rather than create another trust, reliance or responsibility synonym.

evidence.quote: morally responsible for the collateral damage?
part of the responsibility is shared between the programmer and

findings.evidence_scope: The study asks separate moral-responsibility ratings for self, expert and, only for AI, programmer/seller. Human expert receives a higher descriptive rating than AI; paired inferential reporting is inconsistent. These are perceptions, not legal liability or measured blame avoidance.
findings.boundary: Moral responsibility, causal contribution, fault and forward duties differ. Additional actors and non-zero-sum ratings do not establish a finite responsibility share, actual exoneration or deliberate blame shifting.

findings.definition: Willingness to endorse the values or ethical commitments one attributes to an advisor.
findings.novelty_rationale: An existing concept covers this meaning or its boundary. Keep the stable entry and distinguish the present operationalization rather than create another trust, reliance or responsibility synonym.

evidence.quote: such as for the items ‘sincere’ and

findings.evidence_scope: Boundary note: this paper’s MDMT moral-trust facet concerns sincerity/integrity and inapplicable descriptors, rather than directly asking endorsement of ethical values as in the existing philosophical definition. Its human-favoring facet should not be merged with generic overall trust or objective morality.
findings.boundary: Rejecting a descriptor as inapplicable is not identical to judging the agent immoral or adopting/rejecting its values. Mean ratings do not establish moral subjecthood or an AI conscience.

findings.definition: Relying on another as a source of knowledge because of perceived competence, experience or reasoning ability.
findings.novelty_rationale: An existing concept covers this meaning or its boundary. Keep the stable entry and distinguish the present operationalization rather than create another trust, reliance or responsibility synonym.
findings.evidence_scope: Boundary-only distinction: the economic discussion contrasts strategic trust and competence/error-based reliance. The experiment measures capacity-trust ratings and option-following, not a separate validated knowledge-authority construct. Keep epistemic trust distinct from every form of reliable execution.
findings.boundary: Information credibility, operational competence, integrity and trustor vulnerability overlap but are not synonyms. No model’s conscious trust or objective authority follows from the source label.

findings.definition: Diluting felt personal responsibility for harmful conduct by treating responsibility as shared among multiple actors.
findings.novelty_rationale: An existing concept covers this meaning or its boundary. Keep the stable entry and distinguish the present operationalization rather than create another trust, reliance or responsibility synonym.

evidence.quote: part of the responsibility is shared between the programmer and
always the participant who is (reminded to be fully) responsible

findings.evidence_scope: Boundary-only note: responsibility is attributed to programmers/sellers while participants remain strongly self-responsible. The discussion invokes diffusion, but legitimate multi-actor accountability and different rating targets do not demonstrate diminished unwarranted personal responsibility.
findings.boundary: Shared duties do not automatically excuse an actor. The design does not show psychological diffusion, a fixed responsibility budget, nobody accountable or an AI’s felt personal responsibility.

findings.definition: A pattern in which a human operator bears disproportionate blame for an automated-system failure despite limited control.
findings.novelty_rationale: An existing concept covers this meaning or its boundary. Keep the stable entry and distinguish the present operationalization rather than create another trust, reliance or responsibility synonym.

evidence.quote: becoming a scapegoat for the decisions that the AI proposed

findings.evidence_scope: Boundary-only prospective design concern. The paper warns about a future human scapegoat but does not measure actual organizational blame, operator control loss or disproportionate liability after a failure.
findings.boundary: A responsibility reminder or high operator rating does not itself establish scapegoating. Evaluate real authority, information and intervention capacity before applying the crumple-zone label.

source_corrections.location: Pages7 and9–12, within-person comparisons and dfs
source_corrections.issue: Every participant sees both sources, and responsibility comparisons are called paired, but trust/responsibility tests repeatedly report t(854), which matches two independent groups of428 rather than428 paired observations. A self-responsibility comparison is even reported t(936). ANOVAs repeatedly have residual df461 despite final N428.
source_corrections.resolution: Clarify outcome-specific samples, paired versus independent methods and observation units. A simple paired t test on428 people has df427; do not treat the reported tests as a reproduced valid paired analysis. It is possible different outcomes retain more data, but the main text does not reconcile that. Directional means can be retained; paired uncertainty cannot be reconstructed without covariances/data.

source_corrections.location: Pages9–11, distribution test on Does Not Fit counts
source_corrections.issue: The paper says overall/capacity distributions do not differ while reporting p=.0350/.283; moral p<.001.
source_corrections.resolution: At the stated .05 level, .0350 is below the cutoff unless an unstated multiplicity rule applies. Nonrejection at .283 also does not prove the same distribution. Clarify what observations the KS and item-count tests use; do not convert item-level counts into participant-level latent-trait evidence.

source_corrections.location: Pages11 and13, programmer responsibility by order/autonomy
source_corrections.issue: Results say HITL programmer responsibility is higher with human-first and HOTL with AI-first; discussion states the opposite pairing.
source_corrections.resolution: Record the reversed descriptions and require model/simple-effect output. Do not select a direction from the more plausible paragraph.

source_corrections.location: Page11, programmer means and equal-responsibility claims
source_corrections.issue: A main effect p=.0161 accompanies HITL mean3.69 versus HOTL3.7, both SD about2, while model interactions also occur. Programmer/seller nonsignificance p=.393 is called equal responsibility.
source_corrections.resolution: Reported marginal means and a conditional/interacting model effect may differ, so request exact contrasts instead of inferring an impossible result from rounded means alone. Nonsignificance does not prove programmer/seller equivalence; non-zero-sum responsibility is not conserved like a budget.

source_corrections.issue: Methods/flow show two source-specific missions with four choices each; reliance results refer to four missions.
source_corrections.resolution: Use decision position1–4 within each source block. Do not imply four independent missions per source or interpret the short within-session pattern as long-term trust development.

source_corrections.issue: Priority Heuristic authors are concatenated/misordered and pages are409–462.
source_corrections.resolution: Crossref verifies Eduard Brandstätter, Gerd Gigerenzer and Ralph Hertwig, The priority heuristic: Making choices without trade-offs, Psychological Review113(2),409–432(2006), DOI10.1037/0033-295X.113.2.409. A same-title2011 book chapter also exists; it is not the cited2006 journal article. Metadata only, no full primary read.

source_corrections.issue: Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI is attributed to Council of Europe with year2020.
source_corrections.resolution: The European Commission’s official public record identifies the High-Level Expert Group on AI guidelines presented8 April2019. Distinguish them from the separate Council of Europe2020 recommendation, correctly listed elsewhere in the article. Header/record verified; the full guideline was not reread here.

methodological_limits: Participants are nonexperts in a brief simulation with substantial training/comprehension/time exclusions. The final428 are not representative of all850 people who considered participation, real operators, or every person subject to AI-supported decisions.
Rescue versus defense changes domain, actor role and moral content alongside gain/loss language. It is not a pure framing test holding all substantive facts constant.

Both autonomy conditions retain the participant’s ultimate responsibility and use opt-out defaults. Null effects cannot show that real oversight authority, intervention time or autonomous deployment do not matter.

Advice is deliberately plausible and equally competent across sources; it never tests how people detect, reject or recover from clear AI errors. Higher reliance is not established overtrust, optimal calibration or better moral outcomes.

MDMT capacity/performance confidence differs from philosophical epistemic trust; MDMT moral sincerity/integrity ratings differ from endorsing an advisor’s values. Does Not Fit responses are not simply low trust, and excluding inapplicable items may change what is averaged.

Paired-source design, reported test dfs and final-sample statements are inconsistent. Exact inference, missing-data handling, item-count unit and outcome-specific N need original analysis output. No fabricated statistical repair is made.

Responsibility ratings are independent non-zero-sum judgments, with two targets in the human condition and four in AI. This does not establish psychological diffusion, a conserved share shifted from AI to humans, legal liability or a complete accountability gap.

Participant responsibility is explicitly emphasized during training. Stable self-responsibility cannot be generalized to unprompted users, and there is no independent control condition without that instruction.

Four choices per source, repeated comparisons and a late source difference do not identify a causal learning curve or prove capacity trust mediates reliance. Task difficulty, advice type and expected-value preferences may affect decisions; the authors acknowledge further analysis is needed.
Trust and some traits are measured after both blocks, and source ratings are shown together. These are post-exposure perceptions, not untouched baseline causes of behavior.

Default behavior, perceived capability, moral endorsement, proper control and actual moral competence are separate. The authors explicitly acknowledge perceptions do not establish true capabilities; governance recommendations are not independently tested interventions.
Legal/normative statements are historical argument, not a current legal audit of autonomous weapons, medical practice or AI accountability.

source_identity_checks.scope: Metadata only confirms title, four authors, American Economic Review98(1),294–310. Existing betrayal-aversion entry covers the concept. The primary experiments were not read; this is not another independent study credit.

cross_paper_learning.finding: The existing moral-trust entry follows value endorsement, and epistemic trust follows knowledge-based reliance. Preserve those definitions while recording this article’s different MDMT capacity/moral-facet operationalization. Do not merge constructs merely because the words trust and moral recur.

Generic trust in scripted moral advice and multi-facet trust in this timed simulation produce different source patterns. Both concern perceptions, not actual ethical superiority. Human-versus-AI effects depend on task, advice, outcome and measurement.

Matched datasets and interaction descriptions must be checked against the design rather than repaired from intuition. Here responsibility order/autonomy descriptions reverse between results and discussion.

A disclosed preregistration/model correction or retained-sample statement needs outcome-specific accounting. Different sample sizes or dfs cannot be assumed valid or erroneous without examining the actual models.

deferred.term: Capacity trust / moral trust / trust–reliance paradox
deferred.reason: Existing performance-trust, moral-trust and epistemic-trust entries cover relevant meanings and differences. Lower moral-facet trust alongside higher capacity/overall trust does not establish a universal contradiction between trust and behavior.

Separate ratings and a prospective scapegoating concern do not establish nobody accountable, psychological diffusion or disproportionate real operator blame. Existing entries receive boundary notes where relevant.

Already present. The economic discussion distinguishes strategic vulnerability from an impersonal lottery, but the original experiments are unread and the drone study does not manipulate betrayal risk.
Governance/control configurations, not automatically new psychological behaviors. The actual manipulation is deliberately subtle and both versions use default opt-out choices.

limitations: All17 supplied pages were read, including references; no full cited book, OSF analysis, actor-level responsibility audit or live AI capability evaluation is claimed. No author was contacted.
No new row, forced citation quota, annual count or automatic normative/harm edge is added. Source corrections are evidence-backed; unresolved analysis/reporting conflicts remain explicit.
